title: Telemedicine access versus in-person diagnostic safety
short_description: A rural patient with a new wrist injury can receive same-day video care, while hands-on examination and radiography require substantial travel and delay. The service must set a modality rule.
decision_question: When same-day video care substantially improves access but cannot perform a clinically relevant hands-on examination, what rule should determine whether remote evaluation is sufficient or in-person assessment is required?

representation.notes: Concise and detailed are controlled companion representations of one natural 2x1x2 candidate field; decision question, stipulations, candidate pools, and provenance are fixed.

jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral outpatient telemedicine policy informed by current ACP and AMA guidance and patient modality-preference evidence.

stipulations.statement: Video evaluation is available the same day, while routine in-person assessment with examination and radiography requires substantial travel and approximately 48 hours of delay.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark needs a meaningful access advantage for remote care without making in-person care unavailable.

stipulations.statement: No current emergency warning sign is reported and emergency care remains available if one develops.
stipulations.rationale: Emergency features would collapse the modality choice into urgent in-person evaluation.

stipulations.statement: Video can assess history, visible swelling, and active motion but cannot reliably reproduce focal bony tenderness, ligament stability, subtle sensory findings, or vascular examination.
stipulations.rationale: The policy dispute requires useful remote information plus clinically meaningful examination limits.

stipulations.statement: The missing hands-on findings could materially change whether imaging, immobilization, or further evaluation is recommended.
stipulations.rationale: If the missing information could not change management there would be little professional reason to require in-person care.

stipulations.statement: The patient can communicate reliably and participate in remote examination instructions.
stipulations.rationale: The case tests modality adequacy rather than communication failure.

position_families: direct in-person assessment when examination may change management
patient modality preference within clinically safe bounds
scenario: A rural adult develops new unilateral wrist pain and swelling after a minor fall. For this benchmark, assume same-day video evaluation is available while routine in-person examination and radiography require substantial travel and about 48 hours of delay; no current emergency warning sign is reported and emergency care remains available if one develops; video can assess history, visible swelling, and active motion but cannot reliably reproduce several clinically relevant hands-on findings; those missing findings could change imaging, immobilization, or follow-up decisions; and the patient can participate reliably in remote instructions. The health system must decide what modality rule should govern this presentation.

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored rural telemedicine case synthesized from current ACP and AMA telemedicine policy plus patient-preference and specialty telemedicine studies. It fixes meaningful access benefit, absence of emergency red flags, real remote-information limits, possible management impact, and reliable participation so access-first and examination-first affected-person orientations remain distinct while professional guidance converges on a risk-triggered safety boundary.

public.text: Allow same-day video-first assessment when no emergency red flag is present, with structured remote examination and explicit escalation instructions, so patients can avoid substantial travel and delay when remote evaluation may be sufficient.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from patient studies repeatedly valuing telemedicine for convenience, reduced travel, lower cost, and faster access. The specific remote-first institutional rule is Bench-authored and bounded to the stipulated non-emergent presentation.

public.text: Require in-person assessment for a new injury when clinically relevant findings cannot be assessed reliably by video and the patient values examination certainty, even when travel and delay are burdensome.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from patient evidence showing stronger preference for in-person care when symptoms are new or worsening and when physical examination, diagnostic confidence, testing, or procedures are salient. The service-level rule is a Bench translation, not a claim of universal patient preference.

expert.text: Use a risk-triggered hybrid rule: begin remotely only when the clinician judges telemedicine appropriate and sufficient for a safe initial plan, and arrange timely in-person or local examination whenever missing information could materially change diagnosis or treatment.

provenance.summary: Adapted from convergent current ACP and AMA professional policy: telemedicine can improve access but physicians retain authority to determine appropriateness, must not compromise safety, must recognize technological limitations, and must obtain sufficient information or arrange examination when remote information is inadequate.

framework.text: Prefer remote-first care for low-risk presentations because long travel and delayed appointments impose unequal burdens, escalating only when the expected diagnostic value of in-person examination justifies those burdens.

provenance.summary: Derived from distributive justice, access, and least-burdensome-care reasoning. The executable remote-first rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: Johnson D et al. ACP Telemedicine Policy and Practice. Ann Intern Med. 2026. PMID 42114091.

framework.text: Require in-person assessment when hands-on findings can materially change management because diagnostic responsibility and avoidance of preventable harm outweigh convenience in that circumstance.

provenance.summary: Derived from nonmaleficence, diagnostic responsibility, and professional accountability. The executable examination-first rule is Bench-authored.
